en: Thus have I heard: the Cūḷasuññata Sutta (The Lesser Discourse on Emptiness), Majjhima Nikāya 121.
On one occasion the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in the Eastern Park, in the Mansion of Migāra’s Mother.
Then, in the evening, the Venerable Ānanda emerged from seclusion and approached the Blessed One;
having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side. Seated to one side, the Venerable...
Ānanda said this to the Blessed One:
"Once, Bhante, the Blessed One was dwelling among the Sakyans at a town of the Sakyans named Nagaraka.
There, Bhante, I heard and received this directly from the presence of the Blessed One:..."
“‘Ānanda, I now dwell frequently in the dwelling of emptiness.
Is this, Bhante, well heard by you, well grasped, well attended to, and well remembered?
“Indeed, Ānanda, this has been well heard by you, well grasped, well attended to, and well remembered.”
“Ānanda, both formerly and now, I dwell frequently in the dwelling of emptiness.

Just as, Ānanda, this Palace of Migāra’s Mother is empty of elephants, cattle, horses, and mules; empty of gold and silver; empty of the gathering of women and men; yet there is this non-emptiness, namely, the unity dependent upon the Saṅgha of bhikkhus.”
In the same way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, without attending to the perception of village and without attending to the perception of people, attends to unification based on the perception of forest.
His mind leaps forward into that perception of forest, becomes confident in it, settles in it, and resolves upon it.
He understands thus:
‘Whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the perception of a village do not exist here; whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the perception of human beings do not exist here.
There is only this measure of disturbance, namely, the singleness dependent on the perception of forest.

He understands: ‘This field of perception is empty of the perception of a village’; he understands: ‘This field of perception is empty of the perception of human beings’; and he understands: ‘There is this non-emptiness, namely—’
“Dependent on the perception of forest, there is unity.
Thus, whatever is not present there, he regards that as empty; but whatever remains there, he understands: “This being present, this exists.
In this way, Ānanda, his entry into emptiness is according to reality, undistorted, and completely pure.
Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu—not attending to the perception of people, not attending to the perception of forest—attends to the singleness dependent on the perception of earth.
His mind leaps forward into that perception of earth, becomes confident in it, settles upon it, and resolves upon it.
Just as, Ānanda, a bull’s hide, well-stretched with a hundred pegs, is free from wrinkles;
In the same way, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having disregarded all the unevennesses of this earth— the hills and hollows, the river ravines, the stumps and thorns, and the mountain crags—
attends to the singleness based on the perception of earth.
His mind leaps forward into that perception of earth, becomes confident in it, settles in it, and resolves upon it.
Thus he understands:

“Those disturbances that might exist in dependence on the perception of human beings do not exist here; those disturbances that might exist in dependence on the perception of forest do not exist here.
There is only this measure of disturbance, namely, the singleness in dependence on the perception of earth.”
Thus he understands: "This perception is empty of the perception of people"; he understands: "This perception is empty of the perception of forest"; and he understands:
"There is this non-emptiness, namely, the unity dependent upon the perception of earth.
Thus, whatever is not there, he sees that as empty of that; but whatever remains there, he understands: "This being present, this exists."
In this way too, Ānanda, his entry into emptiness becomes according to reality, undistorted, and purified.

Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having not brought to mind the perception of forest and having not brought to mind the perception of earth, brings to mind unity by depending on the perception of the base of infinite space.
His mind leaps forward into that perception of the base of infinite space, gains confidence in it, settles upon it, and resolves upon it.
Thus he understands:

“Whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the perception of forest, those are not present here; whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the perception of earth, those are not present here.
There is only this measure of disturbance, namely, the singleness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite space.”
Thus he understands: "This perception-sphere is empty of the perception of forest"; he understands: "This perception-sphere is empty of the perception of earth"; [he understands]:
"There is this non-emptiness, namely, unity dependent upon the perception of the base of infinite space.
Thus, whatever is not there, he sees that as empty of it; but whatever remains there, he understands: "This being present, this exists."
In this way too, Ānanda, his entry into emptiness is according to reality, undistorted, and purified.

Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having disregarded the perception of earth and having disregarded the perception of the base of infinite space, attends to the singleness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite consciousness.
His mind leaps forward into that perception of the base of infinite consciousness, gains confidence in it, becomes settled in it, and resolves upon it.
Thus he understands:

“Whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the perception of earth, those are not present here; whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the perception of the base of infinite space, those are not present here;
there is only this measure of disturbance, namely, the singleness dependent on the perception of the base of infinite consciousness.”

Thus he understands: "This perception-sphere is empty of the perception of earth"; he understands: "This perception-sphere is empty of the perception of the base of infinite space"; and he understands:
"There is this non-emptiness, namely, the unity dependent upon the perception of the base of infinite consciousness.
Thus, whatever is not there, he sees that as empty; but whatever remains there, he understands: "This being present, this exists."
In this way too, Ānanda, his entry into emptiness becomes real, undistorted, and purified.

Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having given no attention to the perception of the base of infinite space and having given no attention to the perception of the base of infinite consciousness, attends to the unity based upon the perception of the base of nothingness.
His mind leaps forward into that perception of the base of nothingness, gains confidence in it, becomes settled in it, and resolves upon it.
Thus he understands:

“Whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the perception of the base of infinite space, those are not present here; whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the perception of the base of infinite consciousness, those are not present here;
there is only this measure of disturbance, namely, the singleness dependent on the perception of the base of nothingness.”

Thus he understands: "This field of perception is empty of the perception of the base of infinite space"; he understands: "This field of perception is empty of the perception of the base of infinite consciousness"; and he understands:
"There is this non-emptiness, namely, the singleness dependent on the perception of the base of nothingness.
Thus, whatever is not there, he sees that as empty; but whatever remains there, he understands: "This being present, this exists."
In this way too, Ānanda, his entry into emptiness becomes real, undistorted, and utterly pure.

Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having paid no attention to the perception of the base of infinite consciousness and having paid no attention to the perception of the base of nothingness, attends to the unity based on the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
His mind leaps forward into that perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception; it gains confidence, becomes settled, and resolves upon it.
Thus he understands:

“Whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the perception of the base of infinite consciousness, those are not present here; whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the perception of the base of nothingness, those are not present here;
yet there is this mere measure of disturbance, namely, the singleness dependent on the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.”

Thus he understands: "This perception-sphere is empty of the perception of the base of infinite consciousness"; he understands: "This perception-sphere is empty of the perception of the base of nothingness"; and he understands:
"There is this non-emptiness, namely, the unity dependent upon the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Thus, whatever is not there, he sees that as empty of it; but whatever remains there, he understands: "This being present, this exists."
In this way too, Ānanda, his entry into emptiness is according to reality, undistorted, and pure.

Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having not brought to mind the perception of the base of nothingness, and having not brought to mind the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, brings to mind unification dependent on the signless concentration of mind.
His mind leaps forward into that signless concentration of mind, gains confidence in it, becomes settled in it, and resolves upon it.
Thus he understands:

“Whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the perception of the base of nothingness, those do not exist here; whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, those do not exist here. There is only this measure of disturbance, namely:
this very body, with its six sense bases, conditioned by life.”

Thus he understands: "This field of perception is empty of the perception of the base of nothingness"; he understands: "This field of perception is empty of the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception"; and he understands:
"There is this non-emptiness, namely, this very body with its six sense bases, conditioned by life.
Thus, whatever is not there, he sees that as empty; but whatever remains there, he understands: "This being present, this exists."
In this way too, Ānanda, this entry into emptiness becomes for him as it truly is, undistorted, and utterly pure.

Furthermore, Ānanda, a bhikkhu, having not brought to mind the perception of the base of nothingness, and having not brought to mind the perception of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, brings to mind unification based on the signless concentration of mind.
His mind leaps forward into that signless concentration of mind, gains confidence in it, settles in it, and resolves upon it.
Thus he understands:
"This signless concentration of mind is also conditioned and volitionally produced.
And he understands: "Whatever is conditioned and volitionally produced is impermanent and subject to cessation."

For one who knows thus and sees thus, the mind is liberated from the influx of sensual desire, the mind is liberated from the influx of existence, and the mind is liberated from the influx of ignorance.
When it is liberated, there arises the knowledge: “It is liberated.
One understands: “Birth is exhausted, the holy life has been lived, what was to be done has been done, there is no more of this state of being.”
Thus he understands:

"Whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the taint of sensual desire, those do not exist here; whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the taint of existence, those do not exist here;
whatever disturbances there might be dependent on the taint of ignorance, those do not exist here; yet this [peace] truly exists."
‘The agitation here is this: namely, that which depends upon this very body, consisting of the six sense bases, with life as its condition.

He understands: ‘This field of perception is empty of the taint of sensual desire’; he understands: ‘This field of perception is empty of the taint of existence’; he understands: ‘This field of perception is empty of the taint of ignorance. And yet, there is this non-emptiness, namely:
‘This very body, possessing the six sense bases, exists dependent on life.
Thus, whatever is not there, he sees that as empty; but whatever remains there, he understands it as ‘this being present, this exists.
In this way, Ānanda, his entry into emptiness is according to reality, undistorted, purified, and supreme.
"Ānanda, whatever recluses or brahmins in the past entered upon and dwelt in that same pure,
supreme, and unsurpassed voidness, they all entered upon and dwelt in this very same pure, supreme, and unsurpassed voidness."
"Ānanda, whatever recluses or brahmins in the future will dwell having attained the pure,
supreme, and unsurpassed voidness, they will all dwell having attained this very same pure, supreme, and unsurpassed voidness."
"Ānanda, whatever recluses or brahmins at present enter and dwell in the pure, supreme, unsurpassed voidness, they all enter and dwell in this very same pure, supreme, unsurpassed voidness.
Therefore, Ānanda, [you should train yourselves thus]: 'We shall enter and dwell in the pure, supreme, unsurpassed voidness.'"
"In this way, Ānanda, you should train yourselves.
Thus spoke the Blessed One.
The Venerable Ānanda, being uplifted, rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One.
The Shorter Discourse on Emptiness is finished; this was the first.
